title: Piano String Inharmonicity — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Piano String Inharmonicity's rich face, its first round, a Sketch and still a proposal: three walks that each start from one idea and end on a measurement of what their section claims (the stretch grows as the cube while B·n² is small; a bend thins B against a fret by the interval to the fourth power; the string is a convolution until its tuning depends on how hard it is struck), beside the page's own May proof, its reference figure and its bending explorer, gathered as they were. I grow when the page is enriched again; I never hold the entry's words.

offers.what: f₀ in the formula is the frequency the string would have with no stiffness, not the fundamental you hear: at n = 1 the formula gives f₁ = f₀·√(1 + B), 0.87 ¢ above f₀ at B = 0.001 and 1.73 ¢ at B = 0.002. The 'Where' list's "f₀ = fundamental frequency" (and the opening's "integer multiples of the fundamental") could say so; the stretch piece's first step shows it.

"For small B … the stretching grows with the cube of the partial number" holds while B·n² is small, not B alone. Measured on the formula at f₀ = 220 Hz, B = 0.001: the slope between doublings is 2.996, 2.983, 2.938, 2.808, 2.573 (n = 2→4 … 32→64), falling toward 2 past n ≈ 1/√B = 32, since f_n → √B·f₀·n²; the estimate B·n³·f₀/2 runs 3.5% high at n = 12 (190.1 Hz against 183.7) and 21% high at n = 32. Proposed: "for small B·n²", and one clause saying the cube gives way to a square past n ≈ 1/√B. The text's own example (184 Hz at n = 12) is confirmed: 183.69 Hz.

"A bent note has subtly different timbre than an unbent note at the same pitch" is true when the unbent note is fretted, and the section could name it. On a plain steel G string (0.432 mm, 648 mm, 196 Hz: T = 74.2 N, B = 1.08×10⁻⁴), a whole-tone bend gives B = 8.59×10⁻⁵ and the fretted note at the same first partial (220.0026 Hz) B = 1.36×10⁻⁴: the ratio is the interval to the fourth power (1.587), since the bend divides B by r² and the fret multiplies it by r². At partial 10 that is 7.3 against 11.6 ¢, at partial 16 18.8 against 29.6 ¢. A string tuned up to that pitch with its peg has exactly the bent string's B, so the difference is tension against length, not bent against unbent. Whether 4 ¢ at partial 10 is audible was not tested; the page's open question on the threshold still stands.

"The Confusion: Dispersion Usually Means Non-Linear" conflates two separate things. Dispersion is frequency-dependent wave speed, and it is linear in general: a prism, small water waves and a spring reverb are all dispersive and LTI. Amplitude dependence is nonlinearity, a separate property. The click piece shows the two as separate dials: with B anywhere from 0 to 0.002, the string run as forty resonators matches the convolution with the section's h(t) to −228 dB and passes every linearity check, while a drive that makes the partials go sharp when struck hard (0.0005) breaks the convolution, scaling and superposition checks (−24, −24, −28 dB) at any B, including B = 0, and leaves time-invariance exact. Proposed: retitle the subsection (e.g. "Dispersion Is Not Nonlinearity") and say that stiff-string dispersion is LTI like most dispersion, the nonlinear cases being the amplitude-dependent ones. The section's main claim, that this h(t) is a valid LTI impulse response and convolution makes it, is confirmed.

pieces.title: where the partials go · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption: **Does the stretch grow with the cube of n?** One partial first, which moves less than two cents across the whole slider (f₀ is the stiffness-free pitch, not the one you hear); then the row of twelve against its ghosts; then one partial beating against its own ghost, where the beats per second are the stretch; and last the test, on a log–log plot with the slope read between doublings. The cube holds while B·n² is small and gives way toward a square past n ≈ 1/√B. Measured on the formula; the beat rates were checked in the rendered sound.
pieces.near: The stretching grows with the cube of the partial number

pieces.title: the B slider · the May proof, as it was
pieces.caption: **The formula, free.** The page's first playable proof (2026-05-04): f₀, B, the number of partials and the level on sliders, held or struck. Kept as it was. Its header gives real B as ≈ 0.0001 (bass) to 0.004 (treble), wider than the text's 0.0001 to 0.001; neither range is sourced here.
pieces.near: The stretching grows with the cube of the partial number

pieces.title: B across the keyboard, and the bent partial line · a May reference figure
pieces.caption: A reference figure from May 2026, of unrecorded origin: the curve is drawn, not measured on one piano, and its band is labelled typical variation. Above, B rising from about 10⁻⁴ in the bass to above 10⁻² at the top; below, the partial line at B = 0.0008 bending away from the harmonic one. The cent labels below (+11, +43, +94) are those of partials 4, 8 and 12, set half a partial to their right. Its 'bending' is the curve's, not a string bend.

pieces.title: bend it or fret it · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption: **Is the bent note's timbre really different?** A plain steel G string at rest, its B from the coefficient formula; then bent (B falls as 1/k); then fretted (B rises as ρ²); and last the same pitch reached both ways, decaying alike, with a third string tuned up by its peg. Against the fret the claim holds: the fret's B is the interval to the fourth power times the bend's, 1.59 for a whole tone. Against the peg the bend changes nothing. Measured on the formula and in the rendered plucks; whether the difference is audible is left to your ear, with a ten-times-stiffer string to find what to listen for.
pieces.near: This is audible on real guitars

pieces.title: a click through the string · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption: **Is the stiff string LTI, and is dispersion what makes a system nonlinear?** One decaying sine; then the section's h(t) of forty, where the returning click smears into a falling chirp as B rises (dispersion, seen in time); then any input convolved with it; and last the test. The same string run as forty resonators matches the convolution to −228 dB and passes every check at any B. A second dial, drive, makes the partials go sharp when struck hard: it breaks three checks even at B = 0, and leaves time-invariance exact.

pieces.title: the string bending explorer · the page's own demo
pieces.caption: **The demo this section describes, as it is.** A low piano string (C2, B₀ = 0.0005), bent from 0 to 600 cents on a slider that moves in equal steps of pitch; the ghosts stay fixed and the partials chase them. Its sixteen sines go straight to the output with no limiter, so start with the volume low. For the bend set against a fret at the same pitch, see the walk under "String Bending and Timbre Change".
